meta.title: Identify-the-Filter — Diagram MCQs (Intermediate + Full)
meta.source_content: RF-Hub original — S29 Filters Deep-Dive sprint; diagrams are original SVGs at frontend/assets/images/filters/ (not copied from any RSGB/ARRL source)

questions.section_name: Impedance, Resonance, Q Factor, and Tuned Circuits
questions.question: The diagram shows an amplitude-vs-frequency response. What type of filter produced it?
questions.explanation: The response is flat at the left and falls away steadily above a single cut-off frequency — one falling transition and nothing else is the signature of a low-pass filter.

questions.question: The diagram shows an amplitude-vs-frequency response. What type of filter produced it?
questions.explanation: The response rises from a low level and becomes flat above a single cut-off frequency — the mirror image of low-pass. One rising transition and nothing else is the signature of a high-pass filter.

questions.question: The diagram shows an amplitude-vs-frequency response. What type of filter produced it?
questions.explanation: A hump between two cut-off frequencies — attenuated on both sides of a passed range — is the signature of a band-pass filter, used for example as an IF filter or RF preselector.

questions.question: The diagram shows an amplitude-vs-frequency response. What type of filter produced it?
questions.explanation: A narrow dip cut out of an otherwise flat response is the opposite of band-pass — a rejected range rather than a passed one — which is the signature of a band-stop (notch) filter.

questions.question: Two band-pass response plots are compared: one shows a narrow hump, the other a much broader hump covering most of the sweep. The broader hump belongs to a filter with:
options: A lower centre frequency only, Q unaffected
No resonant circuit — broad humps cannot come from LC filters
questions.explanation: Q = f0 / bandwidth. For a given centre frequency, a wider passband (broader hump) means a smaller bandwidth ratio is impossible — wider bandwidth for the same f0 means lower Q, hence less selective.

questions.question: A response plot shows a wide, shallow dip rather than a sharp one, but the response either side of the dip is still flat and higher than the dip itself. This is still best described as:
options: A band-pass filter with poor gain
A band-stop (notch) filter, just with a lower Q than usual
Not a filter response — too shallow to be meaningful
questions.explanation: What matters for classification is the shape (a dip cut from a flat response), not how deep or narrow that dip is. A shallower, wider dip is simply a lower-Q notch — still a band-stop filter.

questions.section_name: Impedance, Resonance, Q Factor, and Tuned Circuits
questions.question: The diagram plots impedance (not amplitude) against frequency, showing a sharp peak at one frequency. Which type of LC circuit produces this?
options: Either — series and parallel LC give the same impedance plot
Neither — this shape only comes from a resistive network
questions.explanation: A parallel LC circuit has maximum impedance at resonance — a sharp peak. A series LC circuit does the opposite: minimum impedance (a dip) at resonance.

questions.section_name: Impedance, Resonance, Q Factor, and Tuned Circuits
questions.question: The diagram plots impedance (not amplitude) against frequency, showing a V-shaped dip at one frequency. Which type of LC circuit produces this?
options: Either — series and parallel LC give the same impedance plot
Neither — this shape only comes from a resistive network
questions.explanation: A series LC circuit has minimum impedance at resonance (theoretically zero, in practice just the winding resistance) — a V-shaped dip. A parallel LC circuit does the opposite: a sharp impedance peak.

questions.question: A series LC circuit is connected as a shunt across the line (branching off to ground) rather than placed in-line. At its resonant frequency, it acts as a...
questions.explanation: A series LC has minimum impedance at resonance. As a shunt to ground, that low impedance shorts the resonant frequency to ground while leaving other frequencies largely unaffected — a notch (series-resonant trap).

questions.question: A parallel LC circuit is placed in-line in the signal path (not as a shunt). At its resonant frequency, it acts as a...
questions.explanation: A parallel LC has maximum impedance at resonance. Placed in-line, that high impedance blocks the resonant frequency while other frequencies pass more freely — a notch, as used in an antenna trap.

questions.question: You need a filter that passes a single resonant frequency through to the output. Which single change would turn a notch-producing series LC (shunt to ground) into a band-pass filter using the same two components?
options: Increase the value of C only
Increase the value of L only
Move the LC from a shunt-to-ground position to in-line in the signal path
Add a resistor in series with the LC
questions.explanation: The component values and their series relationship to each other don't change the fundamental behaviour — what matters is placement. A series LC in-line passes its resonant frequency through (band-pass); the same series LC as a shunt shorts that frequency to ground (notch).

questions.question: A band-pass filter has a centre frequency f0 of 14.150 MHz and a -3 dB bandwidth of 200 kHz. What is its Q?
questions.explanation: Q = f0 / BW = 14 150 000 / 200 000 ≈ 70.75, so Q ≈ 71. Higher Q means a narrower, more selective passband for the same centre frequency.

questions.question: On a filter's amplitude-vs-frequency response, the '-3 dB point' marks:
options: The frequency where output power has fallen to zero
The frequency of maximum insertion loss
The frequency where the filter starts to oscillate
The frequency where response has fallen 3 dB below the passband level, conventionally taken as the edge of the passband
questions.explanation: The -3 dB point (about 70.7% of peak voltage, half of peak power) is the conventional boundary of a filter's passband — it defines the cut-off frequency (low-pass/high-pass) or the edges of the bandwidth (band-pass/band-stop).

questions.question: A crystal IF filter has a shape factor (ratio of -60 dB bandwidth to -6 dB bandwidth) very close to 1:1, compared to 3:1 or more for a simple 2-element LC filter of the same centre frequency. This tells you the crystal filter has:
options: Higher insertion loss than the LC filter
A much steeper roll-off — closer to an ideal 'brick wall' response
A wider passband than the LC filter
Worse stopband attenuation than the LC filter
questions.explanation: Shape factor compares how much wider the stopband skirt is than the passband. A shape factor near 1:1 means the transition from passband to stopband is very sharp — a steep, near-ideal roll-off, which is exactly why crystal filters are used for tight IF selectivity.

questions.question: The labelled diagram shows a band-pass filter's response curve, with a marker between two points either side of f0 labelled 'bandwidth'. What do those two points represent?
options: The frequencies where the response has fallen 3 dB below the peak
The frequencies of the second and third harmonics of f0
The frequencies where insertion loss is zero
Arbitrary points with no defined meaning
questions.explanation: The bandwidth of a band-pass (or band-stop) filter is conventionally measured between its two -3 dB points, one below and one above the centre frequency f0.
